content_text: AI infrastructure investment has been the marginal driver of US economic growth. As today's largest and most consequential capital cycle (others being power & grid infrastructure, defense & rearmament, reshoring & advanced manufacturing), it's impossible to understand the broader macroeconomic landscape without understanding the drivers of and risks to AI capex. So, what are those drivers? First and foremost, intelligence is the largest TAM the world has ever seen - every consumer and every business is a potential customer - this is the 4th industrial revolution and companies are investing to capture the massive profit pools that intelligence unlocks. Demand for intelligence / tokens continues to exceed supply, at a time when inference workloads are growing exponentially. @GavinSBaker made an interesting point (one of many) on @InvestLikeBest that only ~250-500k people use agentic AI today, yet the industry is already acutely constrained. If a fraction of a percent of humanity can strain capacity, compute demand has enormous room to grow as adoption scales. Scaling laws (more compute = better model performance) continue to hold. First through pretraining, now through inference-time compute. So, if models keep improving, why slow investment? Competition. This is viewed as an arms race, not discretionary spend, and hyperscalers seem more afraid of being structurally short on compute than overspending. And from a geopolitical standpoint, economic and military strength will always be downstream of technological innovation and industrial capacity. And what are the risks? Hyperscale free cash flow is deteriorating, pushing these companies toward external financing. This is more of a cautionary signal than it is a negative catalyst or near-term risk. Near to intermediate term ROI for AI's end customers continues to be a key question. So far, improved profit margins are showing up for the sellers (Mag 7) but not the buyers (S&P 493). Torsten Slok of Apollo made the point that in business, profit margins are frequently higher for the owner of the end-customer relationship. But that is not the case for AI, where profit margins are higher the further you get from the end user (S&P 500 operating margins are low double digits, while Nvidia's are ~60%). And while we've seen certain industries like software engineering and professional services drive efficiencies, this has not been the case across the board, with many businesses paying up for AI without offsetting productivity gains - a net inflationary phenomenon. The point: profits associated with the AI infrastructure cycle (for now) are largely being funded by investors rather than earned from customers. The history of these capital cycles is that shortages eventually turn into gluts. While hyperscale ROI is incredible (currently <1 year payback on GPU/server hardware), they are making decisions on long lived assets and capital projects based on spot pricing (understanding that spot could fall meaningfully and ROIs would still be attractive). We saw this in rails, telecom / fiber, shale, and others - demand eventually arrived, but it's a risk to whoever's balance sheet is holding the asset when the price gaps down. Regulations like data center moratoriums that would prohibit this spending from taking place. It's also important to contextualize what happened in July and understand why the AI infrastructure complex sold off so aggressively. A couple of causes, with the move exacerbated by a leverage unwind. Kimi K3 (Chinese open-weight model) scared people into thinking open source would undercut frontier lab pricing power / revenue. The market's question: if the labs slow spending because competition is cannibalizing their economic opportunity, who pays for the compute and associated infrastructure? I believe in Jevons Paradox: as inference gets cheaper, usage outruns the price drop, leading to more absolute dollars being spent on AI infrastructure. So interestingly, open-source competition (in my opinion) is actually long term bullish for the downstream AI ecosystem. Mr. Market moves based on rate of change (accelerating & decelerating vs. absolute levels). Stocks were down partly due to a rate of change deceleration in hyperscale capex increases (a function of the law of large numbers). So, what happens next? I suspect the status quo will continue until 1) we see a meaningful / obvious shift in consumer or enterprise monetization and productivity relative to spending, leading the frontier labs and others to scale back spend (curious if anyone has thoughts on what this might look like) 2) credit markets seize up making it more expensive to finance spending plans. I don't see either of these happening near term. Also, this is not how cycles end - I always go back to the Sir John Templeton quote: "Bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on skepticism, mature on optimism, and die on euphoria." By definition, euphoria is the absence of skepticism, and skepticism about AI capex is everywhere right now.
